title: Cinephiles, what's your most formative movie watching experience?

commenti.body: Seven Samurai in college. At the time I of course enjoyed movies and had seen many of the more famous American films from Casablanca to The Godfather. Seven Samurai, though, absolutely blew my mind and sent me down the rabbit hole of the Criterion collection and beyond. I still think Seven Samurai is one of the five best films ever made.

Lost in Translation was the first time I fell in love with a movie but couldn’t explain why as it didn’t fall into any of the typical categories of movies I’d seen. I’ve indulged in plenty of slice of life films since then but this year is the first where I’ve actually made an effort to become a ‘cinephile’ by learning film theory.

For me it was seeing Vertigo and Rear Window when I was 15.  That was the first time I realized movies can be more than just entertainment, and also that the director's style can influence the vibe of a movie.  Been into movies ever since, and I still love both of those movies.  Seen them like 20 times each.

Great choices, I was on a Hitchcock kick around the same age and was obsessed with both of these movies. Vertigo felt so intense and nightmarish and made me think a lot about love and the difference between real love vs obsession.
Brilliant movies! Hitchcock really is the master
The Green Fog is a really weird version of Vertigo, Guy Maddin made out of archive film footage from the San Francisco Film Society.
This one was so much fun. I saw it at Melbourne film festival. Never seen anything else like it.
Good job seeing both at 15

Great question. I’ve gone through phases in high school and college, but I really started to dive hard into film again after watching two 1968 masterpieces back to back. **Planet of the Apes** and **2001: A Space Odyssey**. These two got me so excited about film again that I’ve been basically watching one a day for a few years now with no intention of stopping.
I have watched 2001: A Space Odyssey at least once a year for 25 years and it never loses any of it’s magic or mystery.  Nothing even comes close for me.

Seeing the Seventh Seal as a freshman in college really made me want to explore the history of cinema and international cinema. It showed me how transportive (and even alien) movies could be, that they could be cerebral and ambitious but still engaging and moving. Had never seen anything like it, and wanted to see what else I had been missing (despite having watched many canonical American movies). It's still an all-time favorite, and I think it's a perfect gateway to somewhat more "challenging" movies.
The Seventh Seal was also one of the first "artsy" movies I ever watched.

When I was 8 I was obsessed with the Titanic, but wasnt allowed to watch the movie. It was on for the teenagers at a new years party, I walked into the room and to my suprise nobody kicked me out. I watched the whole thing. Saw my first boobs, took note of propeller guy immediately, and watched what i assumed was the most historically and culturally relevant movie ever (not far off but for different reasons lol).

Then when I 12 or 13 I was staying in a hotel with my family and they turned on the TV to shawshank redemption about 1/3 of the way through the movie, and I got sucked in. That was the first time I considered movies as "art" and became intrigued.

Then when I got my first access to Amazon I decided I needed to watch as many movies as possible so I wasn't out of the loop at high school. I started to watch Indiana Jones and star wars, then the godfather 1 and 2. Then I tried to look up the greatest films of all time, and the internet at the time had a consensus around stanley Kubrick. Bought his blu ray box set, and watched them in release order. Dr Strangelove, 2001, A clockwork orange, (i had already seen the shining), and full metal jacket really stuck out to me and expanded my mind on what movies could be. To this day 2001 might be my favorite film, and Kubrick at least top 5 directors. Paths of Glory wasn't in the box set, but may be my next favorite from him. Eyes wide shut and Barry Lyndon are masterpieces my 16 or 17 year old brain could not comprehend, but are just as good as the rest as I revisit them. Very hard to rank his movies

I will never forget sitting in Titanic with my niece and there was a boy sitting behind us, maybe early teens, and at the moment when Kate Winslet reveals her boobs he gave this little audible sigh of just – perfect happiness, I would say. It was clearly a big moment for him. I was so glad somebody was getting something out of it!

My answer may be weird but it is Indiana Jones, Part III. As a Deaf person, I spent most of my formative years at the movie theaters imagining the dialogue and trying to figure out the happenings in any given movie due to them not being captioned. I’d have to wait almost a year before they arrived on VHS for home rentals and hope that the rental was captioned. 

Indy 3 was the first movie of my life where it was open captioned at the movie theatre (10 am showtime, mind you) and it was amazing. So I gotta go with that one.

Frances Ha is an absolute banger and I won't hear otherwise.

My most formative movie watching experience was probably LOTR coming out when I was 10-12 because it helped me bond with other people.

It's weird that I never had a sorta film that "got me into" art housey type stuff. I think I was pretty much born with an appreciation for that kind of thing. I mean I saw Ghost World when I was very young and I think I just loved it. As soon as I could access world cinema classics like Yi Yi or whatever I watched them and loved all the usual suspects.

I suppose there are a few that stand out as sort of opening out my emotional horizons. Like, hmm that's a new feeling, or expanding my idea of what films can do. 

Lost in Translation - first movie heartbreak

There Will Be Blood - JG score, DDL performance, story structure

Yi Yi - all of it

Nobody Knows

Spirited Away/ghibli in general

City of God - the spirit of a community as a character

An Elephant Sitting Still - anger

Aftersun

Lynch

Bridge to Terabithia - first full on mid-movie breakdown -- total emotional collapse

Dancer in the Dark. No this is actually the one. I remember because I only watched it because bjork was in it and obviously it just about killed me, but then I watched a load more Von trier. I liked both Dogville and breaking the waves and both were certainly unusual. 

I gotta stop there. I'm just gonna say I'm grateful for all the great cinema out there and how each great film leaves a sort of room in the mind that one can visit. Each room has it's own feeling that you can just go and sit in for a while. When I get excited about a new film, it's really that expansion of my inner world that I'm excited about.

Taxi Driver on hbo when I was 11. That’s when it suddenly hit me that every shot, outfit, sound etc were choices. I had always loved and rewatched movies because my Dad loved movies, and I knew what directors did, but that was the first time I actually understood it. The movie itself felt very mythical to me because I had heard of it and seen so many references (especially ‘you talkin to me?’) and one night it was on…I felt so lucky that I wouldn’t have to ask my parents to rent something so adult. Loved it.
HBO is very responsible for so many of us!

This will sound weird but, The Blues Brothers.  It’s so simple yet audacious, the action musical.  The combination of gritty realism that marries itself to over the top action where it seems like the fantastical and mundane co-exist.  I honestly believe without this movie you don’t get the 90’s Disney renaissance, Scott Pilgrim or Sinners (along with gems like The Last Dragon).

What I want to know however is what’s something similar that came before?

I saw the Blues Brothers when I was 11 in 1980. One of my favorite movies, what that movie did for me was make me learn Blues & Soul music that I didn’t really know before that film. I’m closing in on 57 now and my record collection is deeply influenced by what I learned musically from that film (and the Blues Brothers “Briefcase Full of Blues” album)…oh and I hate Illinois Nazis.
I don’t have an answer to your question, but I am a millennial absolutely obsessed with Aretha Franklin and I think it’s solely from watching Blues Brothers as a kid.

I don’t know why that’s weird, it was the film that was running at every single party I went to in high school, it introduced all of us to that music in the 80s. You’re absolutely right about the quality of the chase scene as well!

Whiplash - when I was like 16 years old, it changed me. Got me into movies initially 

The Babadook - got me DEEP into horror movies after that

Portrait Of A Lady On Fire - got me into “Art house” and slow burn dramas

City Of God - got me into foreign cinema 

Revanche - got me into everything else
Same! City of God is and will always be immense to me
My first favourite movie. Got too many now

In elementary school, went to watch Aliens with my best friend for his birthday. He’d watched it already and insisted we go. At that point I didn’t even know about Alien. From the opening scene of the salvage crew discovering Ripley in the escape pod to very end I was hooked. Afterwards, I told my brothers about the film and insisted we go watch it in the theater a week later. 

Then in high school, Terminator 2 came out and my mind was blown all over again. I needed to see it again so I convinced my brother come with me. After the show we hopped theaters and watched it again. 

Those movies and James Cameron will always be the GOAT to me.
I really need to get to watching the Alien franchise but agreed for Cameron. For me it was the Way of Water that finally got me on the Cameron hype train and I can't wait for Fire and Ash.
How did you get in to the theatre? It was rated R. I'd be amazed that parents would bring elementary-aged kids to that movie heh.

Kind of ridiculous but it was specifically the Bride vs Crazy 88 scene in Kill Bill Vol. 1

It was the first time that I realized that even over-the-top moments (like blood squirting out of a stump like it was coming out of a super soaker) were not silly decisions but were nods to the past of cinema itself. It was the first time I separated a movie from the art of making a film.

I saw There Will Be Blood in my junior year of high school and it completely rewired the way I think about movies. Paul Thomas Anderson might be my favorite director and that movie has so much to do with that lol
Same movie for me but when I was a senior in high school. Far and away my favorite movie of all time and PTA is also my favorite director :)
Exactly the same story here hahaha

My dad had a collection of Aki Kaurismäki's movies on DVD and used to show me those when I was a kid. I especially remember Hamlet Goes Business and I Hired A Contract Killer. I suppose that's where it began. Oh, and also Les Triplettes De Belleville. All movies that I still cherish to this day.

I was ten years old and my friend took me to see The Fellowship of the Ring with his grandparents. I knew nothing about The Lord of the Rings at the time as I hadn't read any of the books, including The Hobbit, nor was I culturally aware of it. I recall seeing trailers for the film but not knowing what it was about, and distinctly remember thinking it was a Biblical movie and Gandalf on the bridge of Khazad-dum was Moses splitting the Red Sea. Anyway, it was a few days before or after Christmas, snow on the ground, and we got in that theater where I was essentially going in blind.

For some reason, right when the opening monologue started, I immediately got sucked in. It was like I was sitting in the darkest movie theater imaginable and the only light was the firelight of the forging of the great rings. I still only rarely feel that strange sense of solitude and warmth and when I do it immediately makes me think of that moment. The film carried on and obviously being as young as I was I had hardly seen anything like it, the wraiths were terrifying, the mood was so dark an exceptional, so I was enraptured, but it was about 3/4ths of the way through the film when it really struck me.

Right after the battle in the chamber of Mazarbul (Balin's tomb), when Gandalf exclaims "...to the bridge of Khazad-dum!" and the Fellowship score swells while they're all running, something in me broke and I knew I was watching the best movie I had ever seen. Prior to this I had no real, critical idea of what made for a "good" movie, being as I was ten and kids don't exactly have a thorough grasp on the language of cinema. Like, I had seen and loved Star Wars by that point, but generally when kids say they like movies it's just whatever is coolest to them and they couldn't exactly tell you why they would or wouldn't prefer one favorite movie of theirs over another. Fellowship changed that for me. I instantly became aware that it was possible to have a movie so good you could instantly become aware of that fact while watching it. I was basically awestruck through the entire rest of the film, from the scenes of the Argonath to the very end, not knowing it would eventually be three parts, and left the theater changed. Even though it was all new to me and I couldn't verbalize everything I had just taken in (my friend and I called Gimli "cannonball" since we didn't know his name) it was transformative. 

I read the books, eagerly anticipated each film over the following years, and my friend and I (whom I still talk to almost daily) are basically foundationally built on those films. We quote them at each other constantly. I reserve myself to only watching the Lord of the Rings films in the winter when there's snow outside to try and make sure I always preserve and recapture that magic of when I first saw them. I'm a huge Tolkien fan now and I'm actually grateful my first foray into the world was through the movies because I think people who read the books first might have had reasons to be disappointed by the adaptation's changes and exclusions. For me I get to enjoy them both equally. These movies defined three years of my life as they were released and helped shaped my interests both in film and life well beyond, and my friendships. You'll always see those memes about "born too late to explore the Earth, born too early to explore the Universe, born just in time to X" and for me X is seeing LotR in theaters. I wouldn't say I tie my identity to them in any sense of the word, but I fundamentally, like in a metaphysical sense, would not be who I am without those films.

This is such a beautiful story I absolutely adore it. I only recently got to watch the LOTR films, and I'm privileged to watch them at all. It's incredible that we live in the same time as those films!

While I don’t have a single stand-alone film I can identify as “the one that made me a cinephile” per se, I do have roughly 3 year intervals I could mark as stages in the development of my love for film.

From birth to age 15 or so, my movie watching experience was just a general rudderless love of “the movies” in which I was just as happy watching James Bond or Indiana Jones as I was watching “critically acclaimed” stuff, which could vary from A Beautiful Mind to Saving Private Ryan to Traffic and even to Amelie or The Royal Tenenbaums. I did manage to watch The Godfather for the first time during this stage. 

Then at age 15, I fell upon the AFI list and started out with Goodfellas, which hit me like a ton of bricks and made me realize “wow, movies are art”. So ages 15-18 were very much my phase one of my “film bro” stage, and my film viewing was far more limited to watching ‘Good Films’, albeit ones that weren’t all that esoteric. During this time, I watched a bunch of the typical AFI and IMDb top 250 touchstones, which includes Citizen Kane, Taxi Driver, Raging Bull, 2001: A Space Odyssey, Dr. Strangelove, Pulp Fiction, Sunset Blvd, Network, Blade Runner, Chinatown, Apocalypse Now and so forth. I also kept up with all the major awards season flicks each year and would dip my toes into the ‘foreign cinema’ well with stuff like City of God.

Then at age 18, watching The 400 Blows and 8 1/2 was a whole other revelation. I’d been given a random book with a selection of 100 or so great films, and along with the typical American canon films like The Godfather, North by Northwest, Chinatown, etc, there was included a handful of foreign films like aforementioned two as well as The Conformist, La Dolce Vita and some others. Long story short, I learned to broaden my horizons beyond what had the highest IMDb ratings.

To be continued, as I don’t have time right now to write the rest of this post…

P.S. There are gaps I’ll fill in later, but I probably didn’t unequivocally reach my film-is-high-art stage until around 21 or so, which is when I began to explore Godard, Tarkovsky, Antonioni and so forth. I’d watched a couple Godard films in a film class in college when I was 19, but I was still ambivalent towards them at that point.

As another addendum, it doesn’t hurt I turned 21 back in 2009 when having a Netflix account both for streaming and DVDs was a formative cultural experience and not the avatar of our postmodern dystopia. A Criterion Channel subscription today just doesn’t hit quite the same way, and I can’t explain why. Partly, I think the evolution of Blu-ray, 4K, and OLED TVs means film lovers A/V standards for home viewing have risen exponentially since the early 2010s, but either way, back then Netflix meant being able to physically rent Criterion movies you wouldn’t find at Blockbuster.
I absolutely love this story, you have such a perfect (I couldn't think of another word) backstory for your love from James Bond to Godard. It's very complete!

like so much else in the world it’s complicated but i think it has to be Annie Hall. it was the first time i’d ever seen a woody allen film. i was probably around 20 at the time, and i knew i loved watching movies, i just (evidently) had a pretty narrow view of what movies could be; this was probably around the time Crimes and Misdemeanors came out (i am an old), and my mind was absolutely blown
Most formative experience was me finding Top 250 section on IMDB when I was around 15 or so, and setting up on a mission to watch all of them. So I basically watched most worlds best movies as a teen
That's lovely! I did that with the AFI Top 100

Watching the opening scene of Saving Private Ryan. For me, no opening scene in film comes close. I was a kid when that movie came out so wasn’t fortunate enough to watch it at a cinema. If they ever show it again, il be right there to experience it.

I was about 14 and was really into planes, helicopters and stuff, so I decided to watch some random war movie with some really cool scenes of helicopters exploding shit just for the fun and giggles. Googled what was good and everyone talked about how this "Apocalypse Now" thing was the best war movie ever made, so I download it and decided to watch.

And I indeed had a ton of fun in the first hour, it was exactly the movie I was expecting. What I wasn't expecting was what I was about to witness after they jump on the boat and start the journey going up the river. After the movie ended I was shocked, no movie prior to that had such an impact on me, weeks went by and I was still thinking about the jungle, about Willard, about Kurtz and his motivations.

I wanted more of this feeling, I wanted more movies that made me think, made me cry, made me shocked. Blockbusters wouldn't make the cut anymore.
Truly a life changing movie. Apocalypse Now does that to people...

It's a handful. 

Star Wars as a kid showed me that there was something amazing in going to see a movie.

Metropolitan by Whit Stillman as like a proof of concept that people can make good movies on a budget. I watch it every year to this day, it's a Christmas movie people!

The Garden of the Finzi Continis is an amazing example of a master (De Sica) playing with the tools of the trade and telling as story that's not the story that you think it is.

The 400 Blows was shown to us by my French teacher in my sophomore year. It completely swept me up, and for obvious reasons really spoke to me as an adolescent whose parents were just kind of never home by then. That was really the beginning of the obsession I think, though after a dormant period it was certainly helped along by the Criterion edition of The 39 Steps, which had me so immersed I just started obsessing over movies of the ‘20s and ‘30s and realized I wanted to spend as much time as possible watching and obsessing over them. That was 22 years ago and that’s been a guiding motivator of my cultural life ever since.

Welcome to the Dollhouse.

It was probably the first non-studio/family thing I’d seen and it made me realize there were people out there making weird and real and beautiful ugly things. From there I started paying attention to IFC (when it was actually an independent film channel) and here we are.

I just remember it finishing and my best friend turning to me and saying, “that was like reliving the two years of junior high in two hours”
and I said “traumatized all over again, don’t talk to me.”

The accuracy of it. The pain of it. Such a good film

It was a series of films from Rear Window to Alien to The Godather 1 and 2, culminating in Raging Bull. All were viewed on CRT TV’s with the first two on VHS and the last three cable TV. Raging Bull was really the one that finally made me realize what a Director and Editor can do and how I had to actively participate to understand what and why I was seeing the sequence of images on the screen.

I credit my parents and grandparents having good taste and letting me watch movies they knew I didn't Quite understand as a kid. All the old planet of the apes movies, 2001, things that you wouldn't expect a kid to enjoy. 

Half the shit went over my head, but I was just happy watching movies with my adults, especially my dad who I had a hard time relating and spending time with. We watched the original Star wars trilogy on VHS so many times the tape got messed up. 

The good. The bad and the ugly will always be a favorite film of mine Because I remember sitting there with my dad who was like "this movie is so good you will love it". I was closer to jr high by then, and I remember the stand off scene so clearly, like a switch in my brain flipped. 

So, if I had to pick one. That's probably the gateway drug I needed.

I really started watching some movies in freshman year of college, watched some Tarantino stuff, Children of Men, Prisoners. Those were great, Children of Men is in my top ten all time, but There Will Be Blood just blew my mind. Only film I’ve immediately watched the next day. Will be a mainstay of my top 4 for likely forever.

When I was very young (3or 4) I had a few movies that kind of mad me love movies

Thief and the Cobbler…this movie had me obsessed with animated films and led me to films like Fantastic Planet 

The Sandlot saw it in theaters during a school trip and it made me love the Theater experience.

The Gods Must Be Crazy led to me looking for other foreign films to watch

Critters - made me love horror and bad movies.

I got really into popular films as a teenager in the late 80s - then a friend of mine wanted to see My Life as a Dog - Swedish art house movie.  I had no interest at all, but I went and it completely changed my life.

I was very young, maybe 10 years old, and I was watching Ocean's 11, and my mom said, "Pay attention to this scene".  It was the part where we see them building something from inside a parked car, and the focus switches from them to a pine tree air freshener hanging inside the car.  We then come to the twist and reveal at the end of the film and the signifigance of the pine tree air freshner and the was the first time i realized you could actively watch a film that the pieces it was giving you could be put in place by you the viewer and that in viwing the film you coupdl participate and it totally changed me from someone who just put on films (which asn't really a choice i was often babysat by the VRC) to someone who watched them and tried to lern from every shot and word choice and movement as much as possible.  I used to carry an Ocean'11 DVD around with me, and shortly after, I started reading screenplays, as well, because of that one scene. I spend a lot of time in therapy dissecting things my mom had done and said to me in the past, but kudos to her for that one, which completely changed my brain forever, but in a good way.

This is going to sound corny, but The Wizard of Oz made me want to take up acting, and I think it was the first time I realized the importance of having a variety of character types to make the story happen.

I saw The Thin Red Line with my dad at 12 years old. The movie ended and we walked out in silence. As he opened the theater doors to the parking lot he said, “that was weird.” And I said, “that was amazing.” And I knew then that I loved movies in a differently way than everyone else I’d known until then and it’s been that way ever since.
This was gonna be my answer. It introduced me to a subtle form of beauty that’s led my life in a lot of ways.
It was my first encounter with the sublime.

I was ten years old. My father took me to the movies. I didn't know anything about the film. The opening scene was of a planet. Then a space ship appears. It's been fired at. Next we see the attacker. At first it was a small triangle, but it got bigger and bigger and bigger. For the next couple hours my eyes were wide open and my world fundamentally changed.
Watching 2001: A Space Odessey in the Cinerama Dome in Los Angeles as a small kid when it opened. I had no idea what I was watching, I don't know if it made me a cinephile, but it changed my brain.

Good question and I don't think I can place it to one film. It was more a general awakening in myself of wanting to seek greater depths than were available by just watching TV movies and renting the latest stuff from Blockbuster.

In many ways, it was getting into those blockbusters as a curious kid which whispered to me about the beauty of cinema. Then, when I wanted to start exploring my tastes I just naturally started digging around for niches.

Back then words like Kurosawa or Tarkovsky felt mysterious and enticing. If one film certified my cinephilic graduation it would probably be Ikiru. I watched at 18 and just cried cathartic tears afterwards.

That's so fair. I remember going to the video store as a kid and just being so enamoured by everything. I remember liking martial arts movies more than the usual girlie movies (though I do love them) cause my dad once rented Karate Kid and watching it with him was so much fun!
I can’t even fathom the money I made my parents spend at the video store. I was there constantly. I owe them, lol.

There was something about the actual video cassette cases too, and how some video stores had special shelves that would display them half tilted. They were almost begging you to pick them up and look at their backs. So fun to be pre  internet and just following your instincts on the vibe of a box; it was genuinely possible to spot the good ones too...

Probably seeing the Tim Burton *Batman* in theaters when I was very young and Pulp Fiction when I was a teen. *Batman* was the first time a movie just lit me up from the inside out, and *Pulp Fiction* was... well... I didn't understand how anyone on Earth couldn't think it was the best film ever made. It shook me to my core because it showed me how much I could love a movie in a way that, unlike the way I loved *The Crow.* 

*Pulp Fiction* was the first movie that seemed to give back and help me understand *film* more every time I dug deeper into it in addition to the humor that seemed to land more with every rewatch. 

It sucks, because I am secretly Paul Dano.
Watching Dead Calm felt like the first ‘real’ movie I watched as a teen. Everything before was comedy or schlocky horror or blockbusters, or tearjerker Oscar bait. I realised I loved macabre drama.

I live in a third world country, and honestly, I owe my whole film upbringing to my parents. They grew up poor and would always tell me how the whole neighborhood would gather at someone else’s house just to listen to the radio or watch TV. They loved talking about how they consumed media back then, before advanced tech and the internet.

I was born in the 90s, so I basically watched technology evolve in real time—and watched my parents adapt to every change. If they had the money to buy a new player, they’d buy it. We always went to the cinema, and even when I was an infant, they’d bring me inside the theater with them. At one point, my dad even bought a projector and screened the kids’ movies we loved straight from the DVD player.

I also watched whatever my relatives watched on cable TV—HBO, Star Movies, PBO, AXN. I’d just observe them flip through channels or wait for specific schedules to catch a movie. I grew up surrounded by adults who watched films all the time, whether they were good or bad. And I’m genuinely grateful for that.

My gateway into films that required more thinking and feeling was 500 Days of Summer. From there, I discovered a whole new world of movies that helped shape how I see things and eventually made me dream of becoming a filmmaker.

I saw No Country for Old Men at 13 it was the first time I'd seen what film could be as an art form and it influenced a lot of my writing/directing forward.  It's a film I still study because of its mastery of cinematography and unorthodox approach to character and dialogue.

Seven samurai. I initially didn't care much about watching movies beyond popular releases. For some reason I decided to watch this one. That one movie completely changed how I watch movies, and what kind of movies I watch. It made me much more open to exploring foreign cinema, black and white movies, older movies, and being much more open to new experiences, something other than entertainment alone.

I think for me it was a combo over a three year period from when I was 13 to 15 of seeing Star Wars in 1977, the Deer Hunter (which was my favorite movie for a long time afterwards) in 1978 and Apocalypse Now in 1979.

In my intro to film class at community college. Pr. showed us the intro to Wong Kar-wai’s “Days of Being Wild” and I was instantly hooked ever since. She then introduced us to the Coen Bros’ “Raising Arizona” and it was when I figured out film could be wildly entertaining, engaging, and just a huge outlet for creativity that people made around the world

When I was 12, my parents bought me a DVD player for Christmas, and the only DVD they bought to go with it was 'Die Another Day' lol (I was a big James Bond fan at the time). So naturally before long I was sneaking into my older sister's room to 'borrow' her DVDs, and one day I took a DVD called 'Fight Club'. I assumed it would be an action film because it had the word 'Fight' in the title, but when I watched it, I was so blown away that I immediately restarted it and watched the whole thing again - to this day, the only time I've ever done that. 

Up to that point, I had assumed movies were basically just Disney and James Bond i.e. entertainment, something to while away the hours. 'Fight Club' was the first time that I realised films could fundamentally alter your perception of the world, and from that moment on I was hooked. I've been obsessed with film ever since.

I watched American Beauty with some friends when I was 16. At the end, we all just sat there is silence for like an entire minute, absolutely stunned at what we’d just witnessed. I always loved movies, but that was the first one that really challenged me and got me on the path to being a cinephile.

In college one of my English professors showed us Rashomon. I’d never seen a Kurosawa film before (my exposure to Japanese cinema was basically either anime or Godzilla films). I didn’t know there were Japanese films like that.

Then in that same class we watched Dreams - one of Kurosawa’s last films. It was crazy that this was the same director. The styles were so vastly different. 

I was hooked - I then watched Seven Samurai and was blown away by the sheer epicness of the film, and eventually watched all of Kurosawa’s works.

From there, I discovered Ozu and watched most of his filmography and I’ve been a Japanese film cinefile ever since.

The movie that really changed my perception of films and got me into filmmaking as a career is Clerks. I was 13 when I saw it and wanted to become a director afterwards but abandoned that dream long ago after realizing I would get nowhere where I live. The movie that introduced me to surrealism was Donnie Darko when I was 11 but the one that affected me the most as a teenager was Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind when I was 13. I look back on it now and wish it was a documentary....

As a kid Monty Python and the Holy Grail, very formative for my sense of humor.

Cabin in the Woods as a teen, really got me into genre fusion (in that case comedy+horror) and exploring more high concept movies.  Been watching lots of stuff from every genre ever since.

As an adult probably The VVitch / mother!  Opened me up to movie discussions and now I listen to a lot of them via podcasts and youtube, enjoy hearing peoples interpretations and gets me to look at movies in different ways.

Safe (Haynes 1995). Some impossibly chic student teachers screened it. To me it is about somebody yearning for ways to be exceptional, and about fleeing from the oppressiveness of banality to something just as bad. The teachers were focused solely on chemicals and I realized they just didn't understand the film very well. For instance, there's a component of AIDS panic in the film that the 'experts' would not have acknowledged.

Sexism too. She barely speaks, everybody speaks for her in the first part of the film, but unlike a typical empowerment movie where she would find her voice she just slowly vanishes over the course of the movie. Such a strange film, I don’t think you can possibly reduce it down to one thing without missing the point.

My Grandparents subscribed to the Bravo channel and it changed my world forever. This was mid-90s, back when they were dedicated to arts and independent film programming. I randomly watched Kieślowski's The Double Life of Veronique and was mesmerized by the heartbreaking beauty of it. That weekend I paid a visit to my local library to explore their collection. It was a small town in Ohio but my god did they have a great selection of foreign films. I picked up Bergman’s Hour of the Wolf which melted my 16 year old brain.

If there was one film that did it for me it was Werner Herzogs The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser. On a whim I took a German film class in college, and the professor’s analysis of that film showed me for the first time how a film can be read like a novel, and how to look for themes that aren’t explicitly stated.

Trainspotting at 14 made me understand there was an art to cinematography. There’s some really creative things in that film/ great soundtrack and Ewan McGregor rules 

city of god was just so rich in color it’s the first film I ever watched with subtitles 

In college French new wave really stuck out to me. Loved a lot of Godard but The 400 Blows (by Truffaut) really stands out 

You can count on me- mark ruffalo and Laura linney are both so good and believable as sibling

I've got a quite few:

3 years old, I see the Original *STAR WARS* Trilogy and *Phantom Menace* at the same time, and I love it. My father buys me a blue lightsaber and I freak out. He picks up a cardboard tube and pretends to be Darth Maul. SUDDENLY he opens the cardboard tube and pulls out Darth Maul's lightsaber, and we fight with it listening to Duel of the Fates.

7 or 8 years old, my dad is a huge sci-fi fan and decided to sit me down and watch *2001: A SPACE ODYSSEY*. It seared into my brain, and I can still see how I saw that ending sequence as a kid.

11 years old watching *THE DARK KNIGHT* on DVD because I didn't see it in the cinema. I feel like it changed me in that moment, and I know Nolan is worshiped, but I can remember that first time seeing it.

12 or 13 years old, I see *INCEPTION* in the cinema, and I fall in love with Nolan all over again.

14 years old, I get the Blu-ray of *CITIZEN KANE* for Christmas, and I suddenly realise I can watch old, black and while movies and like them.

17 years old, I see *INTERSTELLAR* in the cinema with my father while I'm really ill. He loves it, and I love it as well. TO this day, I know people hate the film, but I love it.

Those are just the ones before I was 18. I have so many more: 

-First time seeing films like *Portrait of a Lady on Fire*, *Annihilation*, *The Man From Earth*, *Blade Runner 2049*, *Get Out*, *Wind River*, *Drive*, *Snowpiercer*, *Under The Skin*, *Burning*

-Seeing *Star Wars* return in the cinema

-Falling in love with and seeing every film from filmmakers like David Lynch, Steve McQueen, Celine Sciamma, Jonathan Glazer, David Lean, Chloe Zhao, Bong Joon-ho

-Getting into Marvel and learning I love superheroes, and seeing *Endgame* at the midnight premiere with my friends

-Seeing *The Wicker Man* in an outdoor cinema as the sun set

-Watching *Slade in Flame* in the cinema with my mum recently

No joke?  
_Star Wars: The Phantom Menace_ .
I was I guess 5 or 6 years old, and the third act, the Maul, Qui Gon and Obi Wan fight with Duel of Fates blasting made me love cinema.  
Not movies, _cinema_ .  
Watching that as a child made me realize from a very, very early age that 1) this medium is special, 2) the theater is a temple.  
Now, the movie that woke me for the _range_ of possibilities of this artform to bring emotions through narrative subversion was probably Chaplin’s _City Lights_ . Again, I was very young, but the ending of _City Lights_ is among the first moments I can remember when I felt that ‘fuzzy’ sensation.  
A couple of years later - but not enough, don’t let my parents know - I happened to get a late showing of _Boogie Nights_ on cable, and that one stunned me as well for its narrative structure and what I thought to be a very unusual approach to its subject matter. I didn’t know it yet, but from that day on I became a PTA fan.
Few years later, I’m studying the cold war in school and a teacher recommended me _Dr. Strangelove_ . And that was it, that was probably the straw that broke the camels back (and what a hefty straw that was).  
So all in all, I guess _Dr. Strangelove_ was the film that made me appreciate _every_ single aspect of films: the ethos, the narrative, the technical aspects from lighting, editing, blocking and so on. But in fact, I think it’s a snowball for all of us.

For me it wasn't one particular movie, it was a lot of movies. When I was younger this new fangled thing called a VCR came out. My parents went to a video rental store and would rent a VCR and something like 10 movies for the whole weekend. I was probably 7 or 8. 

It was awesome to be able to see movies without going to the theater. Though I still prefer the theater. I think just being bombarded with with movies every weekend did it for me. We would watch new and classics. 

But one movie finally pushed my dad into buying  a VCR, and that movie was Predetor.  We watched it several times that weekend.

Going to see Parasite at noon opening day. I didn't know anything about it except that it was Bong Joon Ho. It was just an incredible experience and you could feel the tension in the theater for certain parts.

I love this question. When I was 5 years old, I vacationed in San Diego with my family, which was a big deal in and of itself as we didn’t really have a lot of money growing up and so the beach in San Diego was quite the treat. But with that said, I had never been to a movie before in a theater, and my parents took me to a double feature with back to the future and the Lady Hawk. That started me down the path of absolutely loving cinema and loving the moviegoing experience.

There are a few that are springing to mind, like getting the Star Wars movies on VHS from the library and watching them over and over with my dad, or seeing Seven Samurai for the first time as probably the first major foreign language movie I'd ever seen, let alone one that was black and white and 3 hours long, and have my mind blown.

But realistically, the thing that forged me as a cinephile was taking a film studies class in 11th grade, where the teacher did an entire unit on the films of Spike Lee, with a preface at the beginning of the year to show us Kane, Goodfellas, and sections of A Journey Through American Movies with Scorsese. Just an absolute feast of great movies, and it completely expanded my horizons in a way I'll always treasure.
Me and my friend couldn’t sleep so we decided to watch Hanekes Cache, I thought it was unlike anything I had ever seen before and from that moment on knew I wanted to study film at university.

I think I was at university, I was interested in Russian language learning and science fiction, and knowing only that these two elements featured in the film I was about to see I was taken to see Tarkovsky's "Stalker" in an independent cinema. The beginning seemed unpromising from my perspective and given my expectations. Sepia film, grimy sets and slow camera movement tested my resolve. At times I was weirded out, or a little bored. But something kept my attention, I wanted to give it a chance and know what happened, and by the time the philosophical dialogues were well underway I was riveted. Nothing had prepared me for the non-Western cultural elements, the unique use of the camera and location, the completely different way of structuring narrative that kept me guessing, and the combination of something feeling entirely real and mundane combined with the sense of something otherworldly and terrible permeating existence - something at once desired and feared, and so present it could practically be touched. It was a long time yet until I had extensive internet access or many cinema experiences, and with them, resources to understand Tarkovsky, see Stalker or any of his other films again, and grow in my cinema literacy (I can hardly say I understood Stalker for years), but it changed my perceptions about what cinema could be and express forever. It didn't hurt that I was already interested in the topic of religion by the time I watched it. Tarkovsky is still, for me, the greatest.

I should add that my very first cinema experience, long before, was Disney's "Snow White" and that "The Neverending Story" not long after that had what was then to me top of the line special effects, breaking of the fourth wall, and high stakes, and that around the time of seeing "Stalker" I got obsessed with Philip Glass and watched "Koyaanisqatsi" which had its own lasting influence.

For me it was The Great Santini (1979). Robert Duval is larger than life in this difficult story that wasn’t trying to wrap everything in a pretty little bow of a Hollywood hero story. Or perhaps imagine Top Gun, except Maverick is married with four kids and most of the movie is how he relates to his family which is a very different setting than the military side of his life. 

I love the ending. You spend the entire film trying to resolve whether you like this guy or don’t like this guy, and his teenage son gives the final data point in the last scene to put a finger on the scale of that delicate balance. 

It’s not so much movie-magic imagery, but a great story construction and character arcs…which is more of my appeal in cinema anyway.

The first date I ever took a girl on. I took her to see Star Wars: Phantom Menace, but when we arrived, the line to see that movie was literally around the whole building.

So I walked inside and asked what tickets were available. I was handed a paper printout schedule at the desk. The only movie that sounded remotely interesting was something called simply "The Matrix."

I hadn't seen an ad, a poster, a standy or heard a word of anyone talking about it. I went in totally blind.

Mind... Fucking... Blown. What an incredible movie to take in like that. That's when I decided to expand my definition of "spoilers".

One time I randomly decided to stick it out with TCM after Cartoon Network ended for the day.

They played Dog Day Afternoon that evening.

I was completely mesmerized from start to finish.

When I was in 7th grade and staying at my aunt and uncle's place and we watched Blue Velvet together. It was the first 'movie' I'd ever seen, really. It blew my mind. It made no fucking sense at all whatsoever but I couldn't look away. I've seen it many times since then and it that has not changed. It opened up an entire new world for me, a world where people filmed things not to entertain but to get under your skin and make you wonder and horrify you and leave you with questions.

I always loved movies and considered myself a movie person as a kid, we didn't have cable so we rented and ordered movies from the library constantly. Also went on $2 Tuesday every other week to see something in theater after school. I think my first almost-adult moment with a movie was when I saw A Clockwork Orange at my friends' house after school. That movie absolutely blew my mind, I had seen rated R movies before, but that movie was so disgusting and bleak it really shook me in a way I don't know that I had felt before.

My parents took me to see **Fantasia** when I was 3. Opened up my brain, and I gained an insatiable appetite for animation, dinosaurs, and monsters. When **Star Wars** came out 3 years later, my dad started sharing his issues of *Cinemafantastique* with me, plus some books on the making of the original **King Kong**. From that point on I also started paying attention to *how* movies were made.

I was watching some PBS educational show, and messing around with toys or something as the programming went on. I looked up and saw Alistair Sims. 

I had already decided Alistair Sims was my favorite Scrooge ( at that point in time there were only 3 or 4 to choose from that weren’t cartoon characters) so I started watching, and got sucked into the story. It was an English costume drama set in 1912, about an enigmatic police inspector who came to question an upper class family regarding the circumstances surrounding the death of a young woman they all had encountered. 1957, An Inspector Calls.

I was young enough to have a firm belief that black and white movies were dull, but this film brought a swift end to that. It was also the first time I considered an actor’s craft, in my own unformed way— just the idea that the same man could play two such completely different people and do it so well.

The three films that really got me into cinema were Lynchs Dune, Blade Runner and Once Upon the Time in America, I watched them all in my smal Cinema Paradiso style local cinema, through 12 to 14 years old.
It was also in the 80's that I've watched the most important films to configure my tastes and pushed me more to know the arts and to discuss movie making and enjoy the experience of movie going until today:
Paris Texas
Mirror
Blue Velvet 
Ran.

Started with all Avengers movies. I had literally binged watched all of them in just a week. Then started Pirates of the Caribbean...I live in South Asia, these films were actually my introduction to Hollywood movies, they all were soo fun to watch, I remember watching them with my sisters in the evening after school. I'd also rewatch them sometimes cause the fun remained fresh.

Seven Samurai. 

I took a History of Film “art” elective in college for an easy grade - for sure I could get an A in “watching movies” class, right?!  

We watched everything from early Lumière films to Chaplin and Lloyd for the action-driven effects, Citizen Kane for the cinematography, The Bicycle Thief, a Dadaist film that I forget the name of, Blow Up, and a number of other movies lost in my memory. These were all very different from what I grew up watching in my midwestern town, but The Seven Samurai was the one that really blew my mind. I had no idea that anything like that existed. To this day I love Kurosawa films, and samurai films in general.
I’ve say two movies. The big sleep put me on a path of watching other much older movies and the raging bull completely transformed my idea of what movies could be outside of just popcorn cinema.

My first cinephile moment occurred when I was a child. My parents played Singin’ In The Rain and Fantasia on TV, and I was captivated by the music, visuals, and storyline. These films were my initial steps in appreciating cinema as an art form. Another significant moment was during a college course that required credits. It was a film class, and our teacher provided a list of films for us to watch. We had to select one for an essay we would write at the course’s end. The first film on the list was Seven Samurai, and I recall being deeply engaged with the characters and tearfully finishing the movie because it resonated with me. I was amazed by the film’s quality.

Watching Fellowship of the Ring in theatres as a kid had me like Sammy Fabelman watching the train crash. Getting the box sets and seeing the behind the scenes documentaries by Costa Botes showed me that movies were something that *people* made, not machines or businesses.

After that, when my parents rented *Vertigo* and we watched it. It was the first time I had seen an "old timey" movie with golden age actors, phony rear-projection driving, etc. But it lingered in my mind too long to ignore. I couldn't explain why I liked this old movie so much, despite it having aged considerably.

In middle school, one of our science teachers had a bachelor's degree in film before he got his PhD in entomology and genetics research. He started a movie club that would meet in the school's lunchroom on weekends, and the first movie he showed was 2001. He had a little speech before hand where he explained the Kuleshov effect and told us to watch the editing the movie. Again, another mindblowing experience. That was the moment that I realised movies could be more than mere entertainment, they could be high art. 

And then in High School, I went with some friends to "Bad Movie Nite" at the local indie theatre. It was always a mystery what the movie was, so I had no idea what to expect even before the titlecard appeared: "Voyage of the Rock Aliens." Everyone in the theatre was drunk, high, and loud. It was like a communal Mystery Science Theatre with strangers where all the jokes and heckling were improvised. Returning to that event religiously, once a month, made me realise that even "bad" movies could be fun. And some of the movies I saw there were legitimately interesting or accidentally good, like "Frankenhooker." 

I saw Spider Man Far From Home in 2019,and after a ten year run of the Avengers and a satisfying conclusion, I was quite disappointed by the new release. I thought to myself, "is this really all there is? just more marvel movies until the sun explodes and swallows the earth?" Same deal with Star Wars 9. When A24 was distributing such interesting movies like the Lighthouse, why was I still spending my money on this brand name crap with diminishing returns? The last movies I saw before the pandemic were Cats (three times, in theatres, for the lolz) and sonic the hedgehog on a date for Valentine's day 2020. 

living in the post pandemic world, i think my formative years are over. But that's how I got here.

Gladiator ( as a kid ). Rewatched this many times in my dad's study room by myself.
City of God. Just so good and unlike anything I knew. My first favourite movie. I have too many now.
A bittersweet life. The gripping Korean crime movie vibe was insane. It really moved me, and the attitude to life resonated with me.
Seven Samurai. Just one of the many old samurai films I watched at home, chilling in bed,with no breaks or distractions. Great display of storytelling, wit and fighting spirit.
Drive. What a feeling, so cool. The little peaceful moments, silence and extreme violence. When they cruise in the dried out canal, I can feel it every time.

Man I love movies. And this could be a different list on a different day. Of if id seen the movies on different days. Truth is, the best viewing experiences are when you're open to them the most.

I've been exposed to so many movies since such a young age that I don't think I can remember one particular movie that suddenly turned me into a cinephile. But one experience I can share is that, in high school, my friends and I rented Oldboy, because we thought it was some kind of action or kung fu film. My friends were a bit disappointed when it was not, but I was pleasantly surprised that it ended up being so much more. That might be my most significant memory of getting more from a film than what was expected, and as a result, demanding more from films I watched thereafter.

This is almost too bizarre even for me to think it's true if I hadn't lived it, but I (kind of by accident -- long story) saw Stalker in a movie theater when I was 12. I had almost no idea what was happening, but I was intrigued and wanted to know more. A year or two  later I managed to see Andrei Rublev, and was totally sold. 

Also catching 2001 on TV one summer afternoon when I was thirteen. I was at my grandparents who were supposed to be watching me, but they were both somewhere else (my grandfather probably in his workshop, my grandmother maybe visiting a friend) and I was alone in the house. I started it halfway through, had no idea what it was, but was mesmerized. 

To be fair, I was a film obsessive even before this. If, before I saw Stalker, you asked me what my favorite movie was, I would have said Close Encounters of the Third Kind.

On New Years Eve 2000–2001, they played 2001: A Space Odyssey on TV. I was 7, but I watched it with my family and they explained what was going on so I wasn't lost, even if the and I fully took in the visual experience. I was fascinated. It was the most incredible thing I'd ever seen, even if I didn't understand why things happened at the end. It taught me early that movies could be both entertainment and art.

The Double Life of Veronique, watched it for free when I was 16 in our University mini theater. Changed my life—I never knew that you could make a film so dreamlike and emotionally + intellectually rich as that. It started my journey through world cinema and of course I revere Kieslowski and his films still to this day. That small theater started my love affair with cinema. 🖤

Memories of Murder.

Fully thrust me into embracing world cinema. Still remember my professor explaining the last scene of the protagonist looking our into the audience as the killer had not been found when released. Broke my brain.

Saw Contact when I was in middle school. I’m been chasing that level of emotional resonance since. Also 2001 A Space Odyssey in middle school. I remember scouring the internet in early 2000s for analysis for what the movie meant.

I grew up very isolated after I moved to middle of nowhere Indiana from Haiti and I used movies/books to learn English and to help me cope with social isolation.

This was years ago. I was a snob and naive and used to look down upon local cinema(India) while appreciating foreign films. A colleague urged me to go watch Gulaal(2009) which was playing in theatres. I was so blown away that I called him up during the interval to thank and appreciate his suggestion. That made me go on a tangent and entere the world of talented Indian directors - Anurag Kashyap, Vishal Bhardwaj..
I still think about that inflection point in my journey of Cinema.

Watching Akira Kurosawa's "Dersu Uzala" as a young 20 something adult was one of the most mesmerizing experiences of my life. The movie had won the academy award for best foreign film and was showing at one of the beautiful old theaters that were still in existence at that time. Kurosawa spent two years filminng in the Siberian tundra to make the movie and the cinematography was breathtaking. It was a long movie with scant dialog but every word was pertinent. I found out later that it was a true story and now have a copy of the book.

Seeing Kill Bill vol 1 at the cinema when I was in HS. I’d always been a more passive movie watcher, was really in to all the dumb 90s comedies. 

One of my buddies was already a cinephile and convinced me to go with him and OH MY GOD!!!!! It was off to the races from there. I watched anything I could get my hands on. Took as many film classes as I could when I got to college.

I was so stressed and miserable in college that I signed up for a film course just to have one thing in my schedule that I didn’t dread going to — I was not having a great time, and I was already madly in love with movies.

“Hitchcock, Renoir and Godard” was the class and it absolutely changed so many things for me, how I watched movies, how I understood them – I signed up for a film course after that every single semester and had something I loved to look forward to — I started writing my papers on films in all my other classes – all these years later it still influences me.

I still have the books on Hitchcock I bought them too, I just reread one!

The movie that made me explore more foreign/niche/art house cinema was Mommy by Xavier Dolan.

The scene where the aspect ratio changes with the song blew my mind. I know it seems silly that something that simple got me into movies. The choice of music, cut scenes, everything just complements each other. True, there are some parts of the movie that I am not a fan of, or deem unnecessary; but at the end of the day, I relate to the movie a lot.  
  
In hindsight, it was the distinct point in my life where I started looking at cinema more from a perspective of story-telling, than from a perspective of pure entertainment.

It was when I discovered Letterboxd and found out about Hidden Fortress, Vertigo, Pierro le fou, Synecdoche new york, seventh seal. These films changed the way I approach film. I found a new way to interact with film to a life changing degree. Finding out that the medium is more than a product and it's a capsule of emotion and artistic expression.

[***Koyaanisqatsi***](https://www.google.com/search?sca_esv=af5f8747f2276658&q=Koyaanisqatsi&spell=1&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjt_vSXvL6RAxXtEmIAHaAZE6MQkeECKAB6BAgMEAE)  I saw it when I was 13.  It made me realize that movies didn't have to be stories.  It's not my favorite movie by a longshot, but it helped me be more open to arthouse cinema in general. After watching that I was up to try anything.

Blues Brothers when I was 6/7, obsessed, my parents had to take me three four times.

Leon The Professional when I was 14/15.

A man throws away an entire life made of perfectly routined rules (like a monk) because he has let a a kid enter into his life and then, out of affection for this (desperate) kid, sacrifices evertything he has, his own life, to save her.

Absolutely amazing.

Citizen Kane when I was 19.  Where it led me . . . a few favorites: The Passenger.   Wings of Desire.  Werkmeister Harmonies.  Eyes Wide Shut.  Love Streams. Crimes and Misdemeanors. Pain and Glory. Wild Tales The Square. 
Directors: John Sayles, Woody Allen, Jafar Panahi, John Cassavetes. Radu Jude.  Mike Leigh. Henry Jaglom. Pedro Almodovar. David Lynch. Agnes Varda. Ingmar Bergman. Akira Kurosawa. Etc etc etc. 
And that's off the top of my head. Thank you Orson Wells!!
